thread.title: Apple Earnings Come Amid Questions on iPhone Demand and China - Barron's

title: Apple Earnings Come Amid Questions on iPhone Demand and China - Barron's
text:
Apple Earnings Are Coming. The Last Round Left a Mark. By Jan. 28, 2019 6:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Tim Cook, CEO of Apple Photograph by Stephanie Keith/Getty Images Text size
The last time Apple was about to report earnings this fall, it was on top of the tech heap—if not the entire corporate world.
Its market value still topped $1 trillion , and Apple had just unveiled its latest iPhones in time for the typically lucrative holiday quarter.
Then November happened. Apple’s results revealed weaker-than-expected iPhone demand and disappointing sales in China and India. A rocky period for the overall market, and for tech in particular, further punctured the veneer , dropping the company’s value all the way to about $725 billion by late January. Apple CEO Tim Cook created even more alarm this month when he warned of softening sales in China .
What a difference a quarter makes. Analysts and investors are now bracing for tepid results when Apple announces fiscal first-quarter results after markets close on Tuesday.
Daniel Ives, managing director of equity research at Wedbush Securities, says Apple should not be placing the blame solely on China’s economy or trade tensions.
“We continue to believe the majority of Apple’s demand weakness in [China] is related to company specific pricing hubris and execution issues which must be corrected by Cook & Co. in the near-term as this represents roughly 20% of all iPhones in the window of an upgrade opportunity over the next 12 to 18 months,” he wrote in a note this month.
Apple stock (AAPL) is largely flat in January through Friday’s close, compared to a rise of more than 6% for the S&P 500 .
The muted expectations are reflected in the estimates of financial analysts polled by FactSet: earnings per share of $4.17, on revenue of $84.035 billion. In the same quarter a year ago , Apple reported earnings per share of $3.89 on $88.3 billion in revenue.
Apple won’t make it easier for analysts and investors to gauge the iPhone’s popularity because it is longer reporting iPhone shipments , starting with this quarter’s results. But at least two recent research reports suggest Apple faces challenging times for its flagship product, which accounts for more than 60% of total sales.
Chinese smartphone makers Huawei and Xiaomi (Hong Kong: 1810) significantly expanded their global market share in the third quarter of 2018, with lower-priced phones featuring enhanced cameras, much at the expense of Apple and top-seller Samsung Electronics (South Korea: 005930). According to Gartner , Huawei jumped past Apple into the No. 2 slot.
In the U.S., Apple’s slice of smartphone users will be “static” in 2019 at about 45%, according to eMarketer. Android phones, at 53%, are expected to dominate the U.S. market through 2020, according to eMarketer.
